implementation_notes: SQLiteCpp wraps the C API in RAII types: Database opens the file, Statement prepares and binds (including a reused append statement), and Transaction commits in the happy path or rolls back in its destructor, so the message-store structure collapses into a small class holding one statement plus the RAII transaction - no hand-written cleanup, no leaked handles on early return. Payloads become std::string or serialized blobs; the tap is a std::thread consuming a bounded queue (or a lock-free ring) owned by that class, and retention is a DELETE plus incremental VACUUM executed on the same writer, never from a reader. Choose this variant when reporting needs real queries (joins over correlation ids, grouped volumes); choose the RocksDB variant when the write rate of the audit tap dominates and queries are key-range scans.
pitfalls: A Statement bound to a destroyed or moved Database is a dangling handle; keep lifetimes nested (Database outer, Statement inner) because SQLiteCpp does not track that for you.
SQLite::Exception must not escape the tap: catching it in the writer loop and counting drops is what keeps the audit side channel from failing the business path.
SQLITE_BUSY/SQLITE_LOCKED appear as soon as a second writer opens the same file: one writer connection plus WAL is the configuration that avoids it.
WAL is a property of the database file, not of the connection: setting PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL behind a read-only opener silently does nothing, and readers then block the writer.

variants.name: RocksDB append-only audit log (LSM key-value store)
variants.implementation_notes: When the store is a high-rate log rather than a report table, an LSM key-value engine fits better than SQL: RocksDB's DB::Put appends the record under a key that leads with the channel and timestamp, so per-channel history is a prefix scan via an Iterator or a snapshot read, and rocksdb::WriteOptions.sync=true makes each put durable at the cost of a flush (the default, sync=false, leaves the tail in the OS buffer). Retention replaces SQL DELETE: DeleteRange over an obsolete time range, a TTL column family, or periodic compaction with a compaction filter. Choose this over the SQLite variant when the tap's throughput matters most and queries are key-range scans; choose SQLite when reporting needs ad-hoc joins and a query language, and note that both can be operated side by side - RocksDB for the hot log, SQLite for the report projection.
pitfalls: WriteOptions.sync=false is the default and leaves the record in the OS buffer: a machine crash loses the tail of the audit log exactly when it is being investigated.
DeleteRange is not atomic with concurrent writers on the same key range; retention must be a coordinated sweep, not a background guess.
Compaction and WAL growth are operations: an unbounded audit column family eventually fills the disk, so TTL settings or compaction filters belong in the configuration from day one.
Key layout is the schema: changing the key prefix (for example putting the timestamp first) silently breaks every existing range scan and needs a migration.
